title: What is a Mold-A-Rama?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the Mold-A-Rama, a coin-operated machine that uses injection blow molding to produce small plastic toys on demand. They cover its origins in the nativity figurine business of J.H. "Tyke" Miller in Quincy, Illinois, the 1960s Automatic Retailers of America (later Automatic Retailers of America/AMA-era vending) machines premiered at the 1962 Seattle World's Fair and boomed at the 1964 New York World's Fair, branded machines, the company's exit in the 1970s, how the machines work (hydraulic molds, molten plastic vat, compressed air blow), surviving machines still in use, collectors and operators like Replication Devices and Mold-A-Rama Inc., and Tyke Miller's later Golden Goat can-recycling machine. The episode opens with show-tour promotion and closes with a listener shout-out to Jake.

segments.title: Live show promotion and opening
segments.summary: Josh promotes upcoming Stuff You Should Know live shows in Boston, DC, St. Louis, Cleveland and Denver, then introduces the episode topic, the Mold-A-Rama, and a YouTube collector.

segments.title: What a Mold-A-Rama is
segments.summary: The hosts describe the machine as a coin-operated, on-demand injection blow molded plastic toy dispenser, and reminisce about cutting records and Chuck's childhood Christmas angel from Children's Wonderland in Toledo area.

segments.title: Tyke Miller and the nativity figurine origins
segments.summary: J.H. Tyke Miller and his wife in Quincy, Illinois, made plaster figurines after a dog damaged a nativity baby Jesus, grew the business during World War II, then shifted to lightweight plastic blow-molded figures. Miller's company went bankrupt in 1959, and his Earth Invaders and Purple People Eater toys became popular.

segments.title: Development and World's Fair boom
segments.summary: Miller developed on-demand vending machines with Automatic Retailers of America. Machines premiered at the 1962 Seattle World's Fair, expanded to around 150 at the 1964 New York World's Fair, and branded machines were offered for companies like Disney and Sinclair Oil.

segments.title: Decline and maintenance problems
segments.summary: Automatic Retailers of America envisioned on-demand plastic goods broadly, but about 200 machines were made over seven years. The company exited the business by 1969, citing high manufacturing cost and constant maintenance needs; the machines were sold off in the 1970s.

segments.title: How the machine works
segments.summary: Hydraulic molds press together to form a hollow cavity; hot plastic pellets melted in a vat at roughly 220 to 250 degrees Fahrenheit are injected, then compressed air blows the plastic against the mold and pushes excess back into the vat. The toy cools for about thirty seconds, and the machine emits a strong plastic smell.

segments.title: Surviving machines, collectors and operators
segments.summary: Many original machines built 1962 to 1969 remain in use at zoos, attractions and rest stops, often kept outdoors. The hosts discuss a machine-locator website, Toledo-area machines, collector Bill Bollman's Moldville, and a list of notable machine designs. Companies Replication Devices and Mold-A-Rama Inc. still operate fleets, and other operators and a Chicago toy store are mentioned.

segments.title: Golden Goat and listener mail
segments.summary: Tyke Miller's later Golden Goat can-recycling machine is described, followed by a listener shout-out to Jake and sign-off.
